statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (bconline.gov.bc.ca) — integrated OneStop Business Registry e-filing and name request portal administered by the BC Registrar of Companies
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 22 and Name Regulation, B.C. Reg. 221/2002: registered corporate names must be in English and/or French alphabetical characters; non-Roman scripts (e.g., CJK ideographic characters) are not registerable as the statutory name; a phonetically transliterated Roman-script form may be used for marketing but cannot serve as the registered legal name; the legal element suffix ('Ltd.', 'Inc.', 'Corp.', 'Limited', 'Incorporated', 'Corporation') is mandatory and must not be abbreviated in a manner that creates confusion in the corporate registry.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Step 1 — The incorporator may only request reconsideration within 30 days of the name rejection by submitting a revised Name Reservation Request through BC Corporate Online, referencing the original rejection notice and supplying supporting consents from any affected regulatory body if a sensitive token is retained. Step 2 — If the Registrar maintains a refusal, a formal administrative review may be requested under s. 24(4) of the Business Corporations Act, in which the Registrar must direct the use of a name that does not contravene the Act; supporting submissions and written reasons are filed with the Registry. Step 3 — As the final internal remedy, the applicant may seek judicial review at the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 241 within 60 days of the administrative refusal. Name reservations are non-extendable; a fresh reservation request and fee are required on expiry.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Conditionally permissible: the Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 103 requires a registered office and records office physically located in British Columbia, capable of receiving legal process and statutory notices; a licensed corporate-services virtual office is accepted only if it provides a genuine street address and daily document-receipt service; a purely remote virtual office with no local physical records custodian is rejected by the BC Registrar. For the Creator_MCN_Agency industry (unlicensed, low-risk standard), a compliant regulated virtual office arrangement with an annual service contract is the prevailing market practice.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low — quantified first-fiscal-year probability of unannounced on-site physical inspection is 3-7% for an unlicensed creator multi-channel network agency operating under ISIC 7310/NAICS 541810; compliance touchpoints are documentary (annual report filing, transparency register maintenance); no sector-specific regulator conducts on-site inspections; FINTRAC targeted examination is only triggered upon an MSB activity threshold which is not met under the pure TikTok creator-payout model; registry and agent spot audits remain the principal inspection mechanism.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC); National portal: GST/HST and corporate tax registration via CRA My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html) and Business Registration Online (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/businesses/topics/register-your-business.html)
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For a foreign entity requiring national tax identity: (1) Determine whether a CRA Business Number (BN) is required due to carrying on business in Canada, filing corporate income tax, or registering for GST/HST. (2) Complete and submit Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number and Certain Program Accounts) via Business Registration Online, by mail, or by fax to the CRA's Business Number Registration Centre, providing the foreign entity's legal name, jurisdiction of incorporation, registered office address (Canadian or foreign), income tax jurisdiction, and fiscal year-end. (3) After BN issuance, register for GST/HST program account (RT) using the same RC1 or online account; select the method of filing (monthly, quarterly, annual) and effective registration date. (4) For corporate income tax, the BN plus program account (RC) is used for T2 corporate income tax return filing. (5) A non-resident entity not carrying on physical business may need to file a special election to be deemed a GST/HST registrant, using Form GST50 or written request under section 240 of the Excise Tax Act. (6) Obtain a provincial PST account with the British Columbia Ministry of Finance via the BC one-stop business registration (Corporate Online) if the entity makes taxable sales in BC, unless the export zero-rating rules eliminate any provincial collection requirement.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Under Canada's Income Tax Act, no formal 'check-the-box' election exists; incorporated entities are always taxed at the entity level. However, certain elections apply: (a) Section 216 election for non-residents receiving Canadian-source rental income to be taxed on net taxable income rather than gross withholding; (b) Section 115(2) election for non-residents disposing of taxable Canadian property; (c) GST/HST voluntary registration election under subsection 240(2) of the Excise Tax Act; (d) Provincial PST vendor registration election for unregistered foreign suppliers. No hybrid mismatch election exists specifically; treaties and domestic hybrid mismatch rules (sections 18.2 and 18.3 for interest deduction restrictions) apply automatically. Canadian province of BC has no separate corporate election; federal entity classification governs.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in taxable supplies (worldwide revenue) per calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters triggers mandatory GST/HST registration for residents and non-residents carrying on business in Canada; however, certain cross-border digital services and intangible property supplies may have a lower or no threshold under the non-resident simplified GST/HST registration regime for 'non-resident vendors' supplying digital products or services to Canadian recipients — threshold is generally still CAD 30,000 for those 'specified digital supplies', except for platform operators.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not currently mandate real-time electronic invoicing or fiscal clearance for GST/HST purposes. CRA does not operate a pre-clearance stamping or continuous transaction control (CTO) system. However, all registrants with revenues over CAD 1.5 million per year must use electronic filing for GST/HST returns (GST34 / GST176) via CRA-approved XML/API standards (e.g., via Represent a Client, GST/HST NETFILE, or Internet File Transfer). ESR/electronic invoicing is permitted but not mandatory. Certain data elements are required on invoices (supplier name, BN, date, description, GST/HST paid rate, and total consideration). For BC PST, no real-time clearance mandate exists, but businesses must retain electronic point-of-sale data and provide digital records upon audit.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: A GST/HST registrant may zero-rate exported goods under Schedule VI, Part I, and exported services or intangible personal property under Part V of the Excise Tax Act. Eligibility for goods: the exporter must prove that the goods were exported by the supplier or at the direction of the supplier within 60 days of delivery to a common carrier, and the exporter retains shipment documentation. Eligibility for services (including creator MCN agency services): the service must be supplied to a non-resident person who is not a GST/HST registrant and the service is performed wholly outside Canada, excluding services delivered within Canada or to Canadian residents. For intangible personal property (IP contracts/TikTok creator agreements), zero-rating generally applies if the IP is supplied to a non-resident and the exploitation is solely outside Canada. A MCN agency receiving fees from a foreign TikTok entity for creator management services to foreign creators should evaluate place-of-supply rules under section 7 of Schedule VI (unrestricted services) and the 'performed in Canada' test; if services are performed from BC offices, zero-rating may be unavailable unless the recipient is a non-resident and the performance is directly linked to foreign entities and no Canadian consumer subscription/payment flow exists. Refunds/input tax credits are substantiated by underlying contracts, creator agreements, invoices, and evidence of consideration from non-resident parties.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canadian Customs Export Declaration (B13A / CAED e-manifest) for goods exported out of Canada
Bill of Lading (B/L) or waybill (air waybill / truck / rail / ocean)
Evidence of export: port of exit stamp, customs e-manifest confirmation, or carrier certificate
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank statement evidencing conversion/remittance of foreign currency payment from the export sale
Contract / service agreement with the non-resident purchaser and documentation of foreign GST status
Internal records linking the invoiced supply to the export shipment (for goods) or to the overseas performance (for services/IP)
Packing/shipping records and insurance documentation indicating delivery outside Canada
Proof of payment of any applicable export taxes/duties, if relevant
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may conduct exporter audits under GST/HST and impose reassessments denying zero-rating where documentation is insufficient. Penalty exposure: unpaid GST/HST previously refunded may be assessed (clawback) with arrears interest and a 25% gross negligence penalty under Excise Tax Act section 285. Misrepresentation and fraudulent claims may trigger criminal penalties under Income Tax Act and Criminal Code, plus fines up to 200% of the tax evaded. For BC PST, uncollected PST on exported goods/services may be assessed plus interest and penalty at BC's prescribed rates. Export documentation must be retained for six years from the end of the last taxation period to which they relate. Failure to repatriate foreign sales proceeds within 180 days (where commercial practice) may be treated as indirect evidence of domestic supply, resulting in GST/HST assessment at 12% combined (5% GST + 7% BC PST) for BC supplies, plus penalties and interest.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), established under the Bank of Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. B-2), serving as monetary and financial system authority. Foreign exchange administration is functionally dispersed: FINTRAC (Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada) enforces reporting under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17); the Canada Border Services Agency administers cross-border currency declaration Form E311; the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions supervises Schedule I banks; no dedicated exchange-control authority exists because Canada maintains a fully liberalized capital account.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Full current and capital account convertibility. Canada accepted Article VIII obligations of the IMF Articles of Agreement on March 25, 1952, and imposes no exchange controls, no surrender requirements, no conversion licensing, and no repatriation approval for services-export proceeds. The Canadian dollar (CAD) floats freely; CAD/USD is the deepest liquidity pair. Profit remittance hurdles are exclusively tax-based, not exchange-control-based: dividends paid by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident are subject to Part XIII withholding tax at 25% under subsection 212(2) of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1, 5th Supp.), treaty-reduced (e.g., 5% for a 10% corporate shareholder under the Canada-U.S. treaty). Cross-border currency reporting is triggered only at CAD 10,000 or more (CBSA declaration upon import/export of physical currency; FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reports for wire transfers).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory timeline for repatriation, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no surrender obligation on export proceeds. Receipts for creator-incubation and MCN agency services may be retained in USD (or any foreign currency) indefinitely in a Canadian bank foreign-currency account or any offshore account. Documentary retention remains mandatory for tax, FATCA/CRS, and AML audit purposes: underlying TikTok payout statements, invoices, executed creator agreements, and corresponding MT103/MT202 records must be maintained in the corporate treasury archive.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: High feasibility with legal boundaries. Wise Canada (registered MSB with FINTRAC), Airwallex, Stripe, and PayPal can serve as peripheral payout rails for global creator disbursements, fulfilling the target rail 'Wise_B2B'. Legal constraint: EMIs/MSBs in Canada are not chartered banks under the Bank Act and cannot take unrestricted deposits; they must maintain FINTRAC money services business registration and file electronic funds transfer reports at CAD 10,000+. If the MCN merely channels TikTok funds to creators out of its own revenue, no MSB license is triggered; however, if the MCN were to hold and transmit creator funds in a pass-through custodial model, the activity could constitute 'remitting or transmitting funds' under PCMLTFA, requiring MSB registration. Treasury structure must therefore ring-fence principal funds in a Tier 1 chartered bank and use EMIs only for thin-rail disintermediation of creator payouts.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: For a domestic British Columbia corporation with a Canadian-resident authorized signatory, fully remote onboarding is legally permitted under FINTRAC's methods of identity verification (dual-process method, credit-file method, or government-issued photo ID with financial institution internal escalation). In practice, the Big Six banks in Vancouver will accept video verification for the first director and may require a one-time in-branch visit for the first corporate signer at a downtown branch (e.g., RBC Royal Square, TD Waterhouse Centre). Non-resident directors and beneficial owners trigger enhanced due diligence; physical appearance, notarized passports, and remote address verification (utility bills, bank references) are normally required. Answer: remote opening is permitted for domestic-resident directors, but physical appearance is effectively mandated for non-resident directors.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-frequency inbound USD wires from TikTok/ByteDance flagged as unexplained third-party receipts
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed global creator partnership agreement with TikTok; monthly TikTok Creator Marketplace settlement statements; internal reconciliation mapping each inbound MT103 transaction ID to a creator agreement and commission invoice; standard SWIFT category purpose field (e.g., 'Royalties / Commission on services').

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership opacity under BC corporate registry and CBCA 'individuals with significant control' register
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: BC Registry search printout in good standing; Notice of Articles, Register of Directors, Central Securities Register; CBCA ISC register (Schedule 1) if federally incorporated; sworn statement confirming no nominee layers; Land Owner Transparency Register filing evidence if the entity holds BC real property.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Equity injection or shareholder loan from the foreign parent must route via SWIFT MT103 (Fedwire/CHIPS if the remitter is in the U.S., SEPA/CHAPS if in Europe) into the entity's CAD or USD account at a Canadian Schedule I bank. The payment instruction must include the entity's legal name exactly as registered, the bank's SWIFT BIC, the transit number and account number (Canadian rails do not use IBAN), and a clear remittance reference: 'Capital Contribution – [Entity Legal Name] – Share Subscription Resolution dated [DD/MM/YYYY]'. Supporting verification bundle: certified share issuance resolution, subscription agreement, updated Central Securities Register / ISC register, and proof of source of funds from the remitting entity (bank statement and board resolution). A shareholder loan must be evidenced by a promissory note with arm's-length interest; care is required to avoid thin-capitalization recharacterization under subsection 18(4) and deemed-dividend treatment under subsection 214(3) on repayment. Investment Canada Act review is generally not triggered because establishing a new Canadian business does not constitute acquiring an existing Canadian business, unless the activity engages national security review.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Creator compensation and commission pass-through settlements clear via (i) SWIFT MT103 for high-value international wires, with field 70 stating 'Creator commission – Agreement No. [ID]'; (ii) Wise B2B API for low-value multi-currency creator payouts leveraging local rails (ACH in the U.S., SEPA Instant, Faster Payments in the UK; disintermediation removes the need for an end-to-end SWIFT chain); (iii) Payments Canada LYNX for same-day RTGS settlement in CAD; (iv) ACSS for batch CAD retail-clearing of daily creator settlements. Domestic USD-denominated creator payments are cleared via the Canadian bank's U.S. correspondent (e.g., TD Bank N.A., BMO Harris, RBC City National) using US ABA routing and Fedwire. A Commercial LC is not applicable to MCN service contracts because no goods are traded; where a creator agreement requests bank-guaranteed settlement, use a Standby Letter of Credit or bank guarantee under ISDA/Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees instead.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forward (CAD/USD and CAD/G10 currencies) under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a Tier 1 Canadian bank counterparty
FX swaps for managing USD interim cash-flow mismatches between TikTok inbound settlements and creator payout cycles
Cross-currency swaps (CAD/USD or CAD/EUR) to economically convert long-dated creator compensation liabilities

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) permissible only against non-convertible emerging-market creator currencies (e.g., PHP, VND, PKR, NGN); explicitly prohibited for CAD/USD because the onshore deliverable market is always available
European-style FX options (zero-premium forwards also permissible) limited to bank-approved threshold amounts under the entity's board-approved treasury risk policy

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal annual return (Corporations Canada CBCA filing)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after each anniversary date of incorporation; filed online on the Corporations Canada dashboard.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No monetary late fee applies, but the Director may dissolve the corporation if an annual return remains unfiled for a continuous one-year period (CBCA s. 212(1)(b)).

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 27% combined federal and British Columbia general corporate income tax rate (15% federal + 12% BC); 11% combined rate applies to active business income eligible for the Canadian-controlled private corporation small business deduction up to CAD 500,000.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Canada does not offer statutory tax holidays. Effective incentives include: Small Business Deduction reducing federal rate to 9% and BC rate to 2% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income; Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) investment tax credits; BC regional and interactive digital media tax credits where eligible; and federal-provincial foreign tax credit mechanisms.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return; filed electronically via the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Corporation Internet Filing (CIF) system, through GST/HST Internet Filing, or using CRA-certified professional tax preparation software (EFILE).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual T2 return for each taxation year; quarterly tax instalments for corporations with a remaining tax balance over CAD 3,000.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 must be filed within six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end. Instalments are due on or before the last day of each quarter for non-calendar fiscal periods; statutory interest applies to late or deficient instalments.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Report all gross business income, including TikTok creator management fees, commission revenue, sponsorship and advertising income, platform payouts, and reimbursed creator advances.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations must report Canadian-source business income attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment; if no permanent establishment exists, claim treaty protection and file Form NR301 with the payer.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim deductible operating expenses: creator advances written off, sub-agent commissions, content production costs, advertising and paid media, software/platform fees, lease expenses, legal/accounting fees, and director remuneration.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents may deduct expenses that are reasonably attributable to Canadian-source income and must allocate head-office and shared-service expenses using an arm's-length allocation methodology; retain contemporaneous support.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Compute net income by applying capital cost allowance, reserves, non-capital loss carryovers (3-year carryback, 20-year forward), and the small business deduction limit allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For non-residents, taxable income is limited to Canadian-source business and property income; losses arising wholly outside Canada are not deductible against Canadian taxable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculate federal basic tax at 15% general or 9% small business rate; apply investment tax credits (SR&ED), foreign tax credits, and the federal M&P deduction if applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents subject to Part I tax on Canadian-source income; claim treaty reductions using Form NR301 and a Certificate of Residence to prevent double taxation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculate BC corporate tax at 12% general or 2% small business rate; claim BC investment tax credits and any treaty-protected reduction for non-residents.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: BC tax applies only where the corporation carries on business through a permanent establishment in BC; non-residents without a BC permanent establishment should not file BC provincial tax.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing penalty is 5% of the unpaid balance owing, plus 1% per full month of delinquency up to 12 months. A second violation triggers 10% plus 2% per month up to 20 months. Overdue amounts accrue prescribed daily compound interest. Additional penalties apply for failure to file T106 information returns, late payroll remittances, and knowingly false statements.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% federal Part XIII withholding tax on dividends paid by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder; British Columbia imposes no separate provincial dividend withholding tax.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim a reduced rate under an applicable income tax treaty, the non-resident beneficial owner must provide the Canadian payer with: (i) a completed Form NR301 – Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits under a Tax Treaty; (ii) a Certificate of Residence (TRC) issued by the foreign tax authority; and (iii) evidence supporting entitlement under the treaty's limitation-of-benefits provisions. The payer then applies the treaty rate. If excess tax was withheld, the non-resident must file Form NR7-R with the CRA within two years after the end of the calendar year of the withholding to obtain a refund.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic Part XIII statutory rate is 25% for Canadian-source royalties and interest paid to non-residents. Exemptions apply to certain arm's-length interest, non-participating loans, and government obligations. Under the Canada-US Tax Treaty, arm's-length interest is generally eligible for 0% withholding; royalties are typically reduced to 0%–10% depending on the IP type and treaty article. Other tax treaties generally provide rates of 0%, 10%, or 15% for royalties and interest.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 aggregate annual value of non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents; this threshold triggers the mandatory T106 information return and contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation (Local File / Master File obligations) under CRA administrative practice. Even below this threshold, taxpayers must make reasonable efforts to support arm's-length pricing to avoid transfer-pricing penalties.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not operate a separate Economic Substance Regulations regime. However, economic substance is relevant under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (Income Tax Act s.245), common law substance-over-form, and treaty limitation-of-benefits provisions. A BC corporation acting as a global TikTok MCN agency must maintain real offices, employees, decision-making functions, and genuine creator contracts; otherwise, CRA may disregard the structure, deny treaty benefits, and reassess.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly omitting TikTok creator payouts, inflating expenses with fake invoices, failing to file T2/T106 returns, or misrepresenting Canadian-source revenue with intent to evade federal or provincial income tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act s.239(1): fine equal to 50% to 200% of the tax evasion and/or imprisonment up to 5 years. Criminal Code s.380(1)(a): imprisonment up to 14 years for fraud affecting government revenue. Civil gross negligence penalty under ITA s.163(1): 50% of the understated tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who authorized or acquiesced in the evasion are jointly and severally liable under ITA s.227.1 for corporate tax debts; they face criminal prosecution, travel restrictions, personal asset seizure, restitution orders, and director disqualification.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Sham and Treaty Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a British Columbia company with no real office, staff, or economic activities to channel global TikTok creator payments and IP royalties through a tax-favourable arrangement, mischaracterizing service income as dividends or royalties to claim treaty benefits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s.245(2) General Anti-Avoidance Rule reassessment; s.245(5) penalty of 25% of the tax benefit; CRA may apply the common law sham doctrine, deny treaty benefits, and reassess Part XIII withholding with interest and penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for reassessed tax and penalties under ITA s.227.1; participation in sham transactions exposes them to civil conspiracy claims and criminal prosecution if fraud is proven.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Money Laundering and Unlicensed Money Services
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating cross-border creator payouts through Wise, TikTok, or crypto rails without registering as a Money Services Business with FINTRAC, or failing to implement an AML compliance program (KYC, CTR, STR, record-keeping).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act penalties: up to CAD 1,000,000 per administrative violation for entities; criminal offences punishable by imprisonment up to 5 years; FINTRAC can impose compliance orders and asset freezes.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and AML compliance officers are personally liable for failure to establish and maintain a compliance program; they may face administrative fines, criminal prosecution, civil liability, and travel restrictions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Employee/Payroll Misclassification and Unremitted Source Deductions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Treating TikTok creators as independent contractors despite employer control, failing to remit CPP, EI, and income tax source deductions, and failing to file T4/T4A returns.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s.227(8): 10% penalty on unremitted source deductions; s.227(9): 20% for knowing failure; late T4 penalties up to CAD 100 per day per slip; CRA payroll assessment with interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable for all unremitted source deductions under ITA s.227.1, without the due-diligence defence if they knowingly failed; CRA can issue director's liability assessments and garnish personal assets.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Misstatement and Documentation Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length management fees or royalties to related offshore affiliates without benchmarking, failing to prepare and retain contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation, or failing to file T106 for aggregate related-party transactions exceeding CAD 1 million.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: ITA s.247(2) transfer-pricing adjustment to arm's-length amount; s.247(3) penalty up to 10% of the net transfer-pricing adjustment where reasonable efforts are absent; T106 late-filing penalties and CRA technical penalty assessments; possible gross negligence penalty of 50% under s.163(2).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly approve transfer-pricing schemes may be held personally liable under ITA s.227.1 for the resulting tax debts; they face CRA collection enforcement, director's warrants, and potential criminal liability for false documentation.
